title: Air Taxis Enter Delhi's Long-Term Planning for the First Time as Master Plan 2047 Is Notified
excerpt: Delhi's new master plan includes air taxis and air pods alongside inland waterways and new corridors linking the capital to Noida's Jewar Airport.
body:
• Delhi's Master Plan 2047, notified by the Centre, lists air taxis and air pods among transport modes for the first time in the capital's long-term planning framework.
  • The plan does not identify routes, landing sites, operators or a timeline — any commercial service would require separate civil aviation approvals.
  • The transport chapter also proposes inland waterway use along the Yamuna and a new strategic corridor connecting Delhi to Noida International Airport at Jewar.
  • Major hospitals and high-rise buildings could get rooftop helipads for air ambulances and emergency evacuation under separate provisions.

A First for Delhi's Planning Documents

Delhi's new Master Plan 2047 has done something none of its predecessors managed: it has formally acknowledged that people might one day fly across the city in a taxi.

The plan, notified by the Centre, lists air taxis and air pods among the transport modes that could be considered as Delhi plans for the coming decades. This is the first time the capital's planning framework has formally provided for air-based urban transport, according to NDTV.

But a planning mention is not a launch announcement. The master plan does not identify routes, take-off or landing sites, operators or a timeline for operations. Any commercial air taxi service would require separate approvals and regulations from India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation.

"But a planning mention is not a launch announcement."

What the Plan Actually Says

The transport chapter looks beyond conventional roads and railways in several directions. Alongside air taxis, the plan refers to the possible use of inland waterways through the Yamuna, the Sahibi River (also known as the Najafgarh drain) and canals.

More concretely, the plan proposes a new corridor identified as Strategic Link Two — an extension of the UER-2 network from Dwarka toward Noida, Greater Noida and Jewar. The proposal is not limited to a road link. The plan says strategic links should, wherever feasible, be developed as mass transit corridors, leaving scope for rail-based or other public transport systems.

This could eventually give passengers travelling between Delhi and Noida International Airport at Jewar an alternative to private vehicles or cabs. The plan also calls for seamless multimodal connectivity between Indira Gandhi International Airport and Jewar Airport through road, rail or other transport networks.

Helipads for Emergencies

Air mobility appears in the plan's emergency-response provisions as well. Major hospitals and high-rise buildings could have rooftop helipads, subject to building and aviation rules, allowing air ambulances and rescue aircraft to operate during emergencies. This provision is aimed at disaster response and medical evacuation and is separate from the air taxi proposal.

Dwarka's Expanding Role

The plan positions Dwarka as an international gateway to Delhi, given its proximity to IGI Airport and its connectivity through the Metro, Dwarka Expressway and UER-2. Its role is expected to expand further with the development of a 34-hectare diplomatic enclave.

Airport-adjacent land development is also addressed. Hotels, serviced apartments, guest houses and similar facilities are among the uses allowed at major transport nodes. Aviation safety restrictions will continue to govern building heights around airports, though the plan allows ground coverage to increase from 40% to 50% where height restrictions make it difficult to use the full permissible Floor Area Ratio.

Context: India's Urban Air Mobility Push

The inclusion of air taxis in Delhi's master plan comes as India's broader urban air mobility sector gains momentum. Several Indian startups and global eVTOL manufacturers have expressed interest in operating electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft in Indian cities. The government has signalled openness to the concept but regulatory frameworks remain in early stages.

Other strategic corridors in the plan seek to improve Delhi's connections toward Gurugram, Jhajjar and the Loni-Baghpat side of the National Capital Region. With Jewar Airport, industrial corridors and dedicated freight corridors expected to reshape travel and freight patterns across the NCR, the plan underlines the need for stronger regional transport links.

For now, air taxis remain a line item in a planning document, not a service you can book. But the fact that Delhi's official framework now formally provides for them marks a threshold — the kind of bureaucratic acknowledgment that tends to precede actual infrastructure in India's urban development cycle.
